# True or false: Compliance

Auditors, regulators and public-sector rules. Good engineering evidence answers most of their questions without extra meetings.

10 statements (Standard 3, Assured 7). Decide whether each one is true or false before you open the answer. Every answer says why and links to the page that teaches it.

Prefer the terminal? From the repository root, run `python3 exercises/quiz.py --area compliance`.

### 1. Financial regulators generally require a weekly change advisory board meeting.

Level: Assured

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** Regulators ask for control and evidence; they rarely require a specific meeting. Separation of duties can be enforced with branch protection and signed releases, with the pipeline producing the change record. Keep a change board for the small set of changes that automation cannot judge.

Read more: [playbook/compliance/regulated-industries.md](../../playbook/compliance/regulated-industries.md)

</details>

### 2. Links to pull request records and pipeline logs make better audit evidence than screenshots.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** Screenshots are taken by hand, cannot be rerun and are easy to get wrong. Give auditors links and queries into systems of record that they can rerun themselves. The playbook aims for at least 80% of evidence requests answered that way.

Read more: [playbook/compliance/control-mapping.md](../../playbook/compliance/control-mapping.md)

</details>

### 3. One body of engineering evidence, such as pull request history and CI logs, can answer several frameworks at once.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** Code review records support ISO/IEC 27001:2022 control 8.32 and SOC 2 CC8.1 at the same time. Map each practice to every framework in one register. Do the engineering work once and show the evidence many times.

Read more: [playbook/compliance/control-mapping.md](../../playbook/compliance/control-mapping.md)

</details>

### 4. The EU DORA regulation and the DORA software delivery metrics come from the same programme.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** EU DORA is the Digital Operational Resilience Act, Regulation (EU) 2022/2554, which applies to financial entities from 17 Jan 2025. The DORA metrics come from a separate research programme on software delivery. The two are unrelated and only share a name.

Read more: [playbook/compliance/regulated-industries.md](../../playbook/compliance/regulated-industries.md)

</details>

### 5. WCAG 2.2 level AA is a sensible minimum for every public sector web and mobile service.

Level: Assured

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** WCAG 2.2 has been a W3C Recommendation since October 2023. Public services must work for everyone, and accessibility law applies in many countries. Check it with automated tests in CI and a manual audit at least once a year.

Read more: [playbook/compliance/public-sector.md](../../playbook/compliance/public-sector.md)

</details>

### 6. Under the EU Cyber Resilience Act, reporting of actively exploited vulnerabilities applies before most of the other obligations.

Level: Assured

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** Reporting applies from 11 Sep 2026, with an early warning within 24 hours and a notification within 72 hours. Most other obligations apply from 11 Dec 2027. Have an owner, a draft notice and platform access ready before the first real case.

Read more: [playbook/security/vulnerability-management.md](../../playbook/security/vulnerability-management.md)

</details>

### 7. In a public sector contract, it is harmless for the supplier to own the code it writes.

Level: Assured

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** If the supplier owns the code, the public body is locked in and cannot easily change supplier or fix things itself. Contract for public ownership or an open licence. Smaller lots, shorter terms and exit clauses also keep the option to leave.

Read more: [playbook/compliance/public-sector.md](../../playbook/compliance/public-sector.md)

</details>

### 8. Testing accessibility once before launch is enough for a public service.

Level: Assured

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** Every release can break accessibility again. Run automated accessibility checks in CI on every change. Add a manual audit at least once a year, because automated tools catch only part of the problems.

Read more: [playbook/compliance/public-sector.md](../../playbook/compliance/public-sector.md)

</details>

### 9. Separation of duties can be enforced by branch protection and signed releases rather than by an approval meeting.

Level: Assured

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** Branch protection stops an author from approving and merging their own change, and signed releases prove what was deployed. Both produce evidence as a side effect of normal work. A meeting adds delay without adding that evidence.

Read more: [playbook/compliance/regulated-industries.md](../../playbook/compliance/regulated-industries.md)

</details>

### 10. A government service team should be disbanded once the service launches.

Level: Assured

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** A live service needs fixes, security updates and improvements for as long as citizens use it. Disbanding the team leaves it to decay until an expensive replacement project. Fund a persistent service team instead.

Read more: [playbook/compliance/public-sector.md](../../playbook/compliance/public-sector.md)

</details>
